chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
title: Firing Amos Woodruff and Alexander's reaction
summary: Fields lets Amos go to please his section and Rene Hall, then Alexander on the phone is aghast.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Oh, yes, he could follow it very good.
He read slow?
Yes. So anyway, the guys would hum and hum, we finally got a break, are you going to carry Amos up there and embarass us?
To New York?
Yeah, to New York and everything.
The Big Apple?

Yeah, the Big Apple. (Inaudible) Ernie finally got a break, the man that's got Count Basie is carrying Ernie to New York, and he's going to embarass us like that and at first I didn't pay any attention to it, then I began to think about what Alexander had told me; anybody can't be fired and maybe these guys and I got a little ego myself, well maybe I better let them know right quick who's boss and I've been drilling

(inaudible) and here you got a man you know can't read and you're going to carry him along with you. So anyway I got to talking to my arranger, Rene Hall,--Edward Milton did some, but Rene was Rene was one that was the hardest; that's the only run-in I would have. I wasn't an arranger but I used to raise the devil with Rene about so many notes that didn't mean anything in his arrangements.
Over arranged?
Yeah.

And so he told me, he said, I'll tell you what, I don't think any of your arrangements arrange as hard as me, but Amos finally gets it and when he gets it he's got it, you know, and I think you shouldn't worry about that. I was talking to Harry Garnett, there wasn't anybody there in Tulsa that I knew that I could get, or in the area, and Harry Garnett, he was one that played, I found out later, why Alexander liked the band so, he was on the style of Herschel Evans, at that time,

and Bud Douglas, another tenor man was something like Pres, and so they just knocked him out. So anyway, he said I know a man in Chicago I can get, play anything you have in your book--that's Harry Garnett--but I don't know if he would fit like Amos; Amos sure fit this band good. And I finally decided I better give him his notice while I got time. So I gave Amos the notice and of course he was going around like he lost his mother or something; all the rest of the band just grinning and this young man came in and just like Harry Garnett said, he just put the book down--
What was his name?
I forget what his name was, because he was there such a little time.
So I was in Tyler, Texas and we played one date there and since we weren't travelling, we were having rehearsal while we were in there, and one of the guys said, what have
you heard from Alexander and I said (inaudible) and I said I believe I better give Alexander a buzz.
So I called Alexander from Tyler, Texas and I said, haven't heard from you in a good while, when do you think you're going to get us going and he said well, I think (inaudible)--
I played there with Basie, several times.

I just wanted to get things straight and he said you got nothing to worry about, go ahead and rehearse; the band is good, but there's always room for improvement. I said yes, I'm rehearsing everyday if I'm not travelling and I said I even made a change in the band. He said made a change in the band? I said yes, I let Amos Woodruff go, he read so bad and everything and he said I don't know anything about anybody's name in the band, but Fields, I have a very good picture of your group, what did Amos play? I said heavy set
dark trumpet player, sat in the middle. The man almost jumped through the telephone--
(Side B of Tape 2 ended at this point. Transcript will continue in accordance with Tape 3.)
